content: Subpial transection surgery is a procedure considered for patients with epilepsy that does not respond to antiepileptic drugs (AEDs). Approximately 30% of individuals with epilepsy continue to experience seizures despite trying multiple AEDs. These patients are classified as having refractory or uncontrolled epilepsy. Although there is no universally agreed-upon definition of refractory epilepsy, for the purposes of this review, epilepsy is considered drug-resistant if seizures persist after the failure of at least two AEDs. Experts suggest that early surgical intervention may help control seizures at a younger age, potentially improving the intellectual and social development of children. Among the various surgical options available for treating refractory epilepsy, subpial transection is one such procedure. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of subpial transection surgery on focal-onset seizures and generalized tonic-clonic seizures in both children and adults. To gather evidence, a comprehensive search was conducted on August 7, 2018, across several databases, including the Cochrane Register of Studies (CRS Web), MEDLINE, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP). No restrictions were placed on language during the search. The review considered all randomized and quasi-randomized parallel-group studies, regardless of whether they were blinded or non-blinded. Two independent reviewers screened the identified trials. They also planned to assess the methodological quality of the studies and extract data independently if relevant studies were found. However, the search did not identify any studies that met the inclusion criteria. As a result, no evidence was found to either support or refute the use of subpial transection surgery for patients with medically refractory epilepsy. The authors concluded that there is a lack of evidence regarding the effectiveness of subpial transection surgery for this patient population. They emphasized the need for well-designed randomized controlled trials to provide guidance for clinical practice.
